clue.text: Public displays bring things to light endlessly

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the phrase's word is cut off

blocks.note: to expose is to reveal what was hidden

explanation.surface: Public shows that reveal hidden matters without ever quite finishing.
explanation.definitionFit: Expos are large exhibitions or trade fairs, short for expositions, staged for the general public.

clue.text: Haphazard topping of trees, losing the first pair, not seen here?

definitions.note: cryptic: you cannot see the forest for the trees

indicators.note: something haphazard is arranged at random, so the letters are jumbled
the opening two letters of the phrase are to be dropped before anything else happens

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Careless pruning of trees in some place you cannot spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Epping Forest is an ancient woodland on the edge of London. The question alludes to the saying about not seeing the wood for the trees.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says people sometimes cannot see the forest for its trees, so a forest is jokingly what goes unseen.

clue.text: Container to discharge right one for a collection

blocks.note: a pot holds things
to pour is to let liquid flow out
R is the abbreviation for right
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Instructions to empty a vessel properly to make a collection.
explanation.definitionFit: A potpourri is a miscellaneous mixture or medley of assorted items, as of music or writings.

clue.text: Teams from the Borders

blocks.note: first meaning: opposing groups in a game
second meaning: the edges of something

explanation.surface: Sports teams coming from the Borders region of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Borders is a region of southern Scotland famous for rugby, which makes the clue look geographical.
explanation.definitionFit: Sides are both rival teams in a match and the edges or margins of a shape.

clue.text: Take this to get a balanced perspective

definitions.text: Take this to get a balanced perspective

blocks.clueFragment: Take this to get a balanced perspective
blocks.note: surface reading: advice to stand back and judge calmly
setter's reading: the idiom take the something view means consider long-term consequences

explanation.walkthrough: The clue simply completes a familiar idiom about thinking ahead rather than reacting.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking the long view means considering distant consequences instead of immediate ones, which yields balanced judgement.

clue.text: One of the Beach Boys?

blocks.note: surface reading: a member of the Californian pop group
setter's reading: men employed at a beach to watch over swimmers

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point to the band, but the clue means any man who works on a beach.
explanation.definitionFit: This person patrols a beach or pool to rescue swimmers in difficulty, so is literally a beach worker.

clue.text: There's nothing containing a fastening device

indicators.note: containing says one piece sits wrapped inside the other

blocks.note: nil means zero
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that no fastener of any kind is available.
explanation.definitionFit: A nail is a metal spike hammered in to join pieces of wood, so it fastens things.

clue.text: Gave betel nuts as a food plant

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone handed over betel nuts, treating them as a crop to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: Betel nuts are real, which makes nuts look like a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: A vegetable is any plant, or plant part, grown and eaten as food.

clue.text: Cut out periods with English

blocks.note: eras are spans of history
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A timetable revision dropping lessons in history periods along with English.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to remove or delete something completely, wiping it out of a record.

clue.text: Pie of sage rated surprisingly as a delicacy

indicators.note: a surprising result comes out in an unexpected form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sage-flavoured pie unexpectedly judged a gourmet treat.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed key spells the French word as FOIS; the dish is foie gras, meaning fat liver, and the letters supplied give FOIE.
explanation.definitionFit: This French paste of fattened goose or duck liver is a costly luxury food.

clue.text: Having been in a  "no win" situation?

definitions.text: Having been in a  "no win" situation?

blocks.clueFragment: Having been in a  "no win" situation?
blocks.note: surface reading: trapped in a predicament with no good outcome
setter's reading: simply having had no victory at all

explanation.walkthrough: A no-win situation usually means a dilemma; here it is taken literally as failing to win.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has achieved no win has failed, which is what lacking success means.

clue.text: Sing one unusual note in advertising medium

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the words are put into a strange order

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A singer performs an odd note in a television commercial.
explanation.definitionFit: Glowing gas-filled tubes shaped into words are used to advertise shops and bars.

clue.text: Spread bad news about trustee

indicators.note: bad suggests something gone wrong, so the letters are scrambled
about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Tr is the abbreviation for trustee

explanation.surface: Someone spreading damaging gossip about the trustee of a fund.
explanation.definitionFit: Strewn means scattered over a surface, the past participle of a verb meaning to scatter.

clue.text: Warning from company about true article

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps the following pair

blocks.note: a firm is a business
real means genuine
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A firm issuing a caution about a genuine news item.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell or siren that sounds to signal an outbreak of flames is a warning device.

clue.text: Redecorate room in gold, scheming with affection

indicators.note: redecorating rearranges a space, so the letters are reordered
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
sly means cunning

explanation.surface: Plotting to do up a room in gold, with loving care.
explanation.definitionFit: Amorously means in a loving or romantic manner, showing desire and fondness.

clue.text: Dine twice in Merton? Not half! But he's not a vegetarian

indicators.note: not half says one half of the college name is dropped
in places the repeated verb inside the remaining letters

blocks.note: eat means dine, written two times
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner at Merton College, eating double helpings, insists he is no vegetarian.
explanation.walkthrough: Merton is an Oxford college; only its first half, MER, is kept and the doubled verb goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who eats animal flesh, a carnivore, is by definition not a vegetarian.

clue.text: In this cab I journey in comfort, being small and elegant

indicators.note: in says the letters lie inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across cab, I and journey
surface padding that completes the picture of a pleasant ride

explanation.surface: Travelling comfortably in a dainty, stylish taxi.
explanation.definitionFit: Bijou, borrowed from French for jewel, describes something small but tastefully elegant, like a cottage.

clue.text: Throws overboard as plane sits on waves

indicators.note: waves set things moving and tossing, so the letters are churned

blocks.note: a jet is an aircraft
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cargo dumped into the sea while an aircraft rests on the water.
explanation.definitionFit: To jettison is to discard cargo from a ship or aircraft to lighten it.

clue.text: There's money, perhaps, in a zoo

definitions.note: an example of what is found there, signalled by perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: old British slang for cash
second meaning: a large horned animal kept in a zoo

explanation.surface: Somebody suspects zoos are lucrative businesses.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhino is dated British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a slang term for cash and the short name of the horned rhinoceros seen at zoos.

clue.text: Telephone introduces 'eated debate

indicators.note: the apostrophe shows a dropped initial aitch, so the matching word loses its H too

blocks.note: to dial is to phone
heated, frantic

explanation.surface: A phone call opens a heated argument, said in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech drops the H, so the synonym for heated is written without it too.
explanation.definitionFit: Dialectic is the art of reasoned argument, investigating truth by the discussion of opposing views.

clue.text: Dry hill region

blocks.note: sec is the wine term for dry
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: An arid upland area.
explanation.definitionFit: A sector is a distinct area or zone, such as a part of a city.

clue.text: Councillor with boring item to move hesitatingly

blocks.note: Cr is the abbreviation for councillor
an awl is a tool for piercing holes

explanation.surface: A dull local politician shuffles along reluctantly.
explanation.definitionFit: To crawl is to proceed very slowly, inching along as if on hands and knees.

clue.text: Local girl's a hit, almost

blocks.note: near means close by
a miss is a young woman

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood girl has very nearly become a success.
explanation.definitionFit: A near miss is a shot or collision that just fails to connect, so it nearly struck.

clue.text: Pipes for the roof?

definitions.note: describes the material rather than naming it

blocks.note: first meaning: simple wind instruments or tubes cut from hollow stalks
second meaning: stalks used to thatch a roof

explanation.walkthrough: Pipes and roofs suggest plumbing; instead both meanings come from the same waterside plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Hollow stalks of this marsh grass are made into pan-pipes and laid as thatch on cottages.

clue.text: Cause downfall of a sound organisation

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of sound and the start of organisation

explanation.surface: Bringing about the collapse of a financially healthy organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no word telling you to look inside; the phrase 'sound organisation' simply conceals the answer across its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo someone is to ruin them or bring about their failure, as in 'pride was his undoing'.

clue.text: Protesting excessively but getting tremendous  applause

blocks.note: first meaning: complaining very loudly
second meaning: an audience cheering wildly

explanation.surface: An objector makes a fuss yet earns a huge ovation.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes making a great noise, whether angry complaint or wild cheering from a crowd.

clue.text: Actor filled with energy by theatre fan

indicators.note: filled with means something is placed inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: a player performs on stage
go means vigour

explanation.surface: A performer energised by an admirer in the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who regularly attends live drama performances is a lover of the stage.

clue.text: Ropy material is in public auction, mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
in places the small word inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a sale where goods go to the highest bidder

explanation.surface: Fibre being offered in an open auction.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a stiff fibre from an agave plant, twisted into rope and twine.
